name: Nana Kwesi's Hand-Knit Cable Pullover
description:
Not a brand. Not a product line. Just a sweater knitted by an elderly man named Kwesi Asamoah-Lindqvist who lives in a Tier 2 residential block in the north corridor and sells his work through a small table at the weekend market near the Halsted transit hub. The cable pattern is his own design — a dense, Aran-adjacent structure with a West African geometric accent along the yoke that he developed over forty years of knitting. The yarn is a commercial wool-acrylic blend in whatever colors were available at the supply co-op that week.

The sweaters are heavy, warm, and irregular in the way that handmade things are irregular — a sleeve slightly longer, a collar that sits a little higher on one side. Each one is unique. He sells maybe one or two a week, mostly to regulars who've been buying from him for years. They last. People hand them down.
materials: yoke geometric accent in contrasting color
what_it_says: Someone made this for you, or you found something real at a market and had the sense to buy it.
worn_by: people who knew Kwesi or were referred to him
story_hooks: Kwesi has been knitting since before the city's current tier system solidified. He knows things about old neighborhoods that don't exist anymore, and he talks while he works.
One of his sweaters was worn in a widely-circulated photograph from a significant moment in recent city history. He doesn't know. The person wearing it does.
Kwesi is getting old and his hands are starting to hurt. His regular customers are quietly trying to figure out who will carry on the pattern, and whether that's even possible.
